title: Projects
text:
The posts on this site are arguments. These are artifacts: code that someone other than me runs, or was built to be handed over. Each one links to its source.
Where a project produced a result, the result is stated here rather than implied — including where the answer was less clean than I wanted.

title: Projects
text:
Research and modelling

Messi vs Ronaldo — the weighted case





An R Shiny dashboard that compares the two on difficulty-adjusted scoring rather than raw totals. Opponent Elo, venue, competition stage and away status are compressed into one difficulty score by a single global FAMD, and goals are weighted by it. The denominator is every valid minute — 2,201 appearances and 181,081 minutes, with all 1,063 scoreless appearances kept in, which is where most comparisons quietly cheat.
The result is the reason the project is worth reading. On the weighted index per 90 the gap is +0.0953 in Messi’s favour (0.1337 against 0.0384), and a seeded 10,000-resample match bootstrap puts 96% of resampled differences above zero — but the 95% percentile interval is [−0.0120, +0.1999], which crosses it. The dashboard reports both numbers side by side and refuses to print a significance verdict or a winner badge. Cohen’s d is +0.090.
It is a fixed 2002–2026 research snapshot, not a live feed of career totals, and the limitations section says so in seven bullets. Runs from a precomputed bundle rather than scraping at startup; the container is pinned by digest and runs non-root.
Open the live dashboard




Bayesian Change-Point Detection in Nigerian Rainfall





A hierarchical Bayesian change-point analysis of 74 years of precipitation (1950–2023) across nine meteorological stations in Nigeria’s three climate zones, written for an IEEE conference paper. PyMC and NUTS, with partial pooling of change-point timing across zones through shared hyperpriors and a non-centered parameterisation.
The finding worth stating: the transitions are coherent but asynchronous — Sahel breaks in 1958, Guinea Savanna in 2016, Coastal in 2015, with the hierarchical group estimate at 1989. The Coastal 94% HDI spans 1996–2022, which is wide enough to be honest about how little that zone’s timing is pinned down. The no-change-point null is decisively rejected in every zone by PSIS-LOO.
Priors are weakly informative and each one is justified in a table in the README. Pre-computed MCMC traces ship with the repository, so the figures can be regenerated without re-running the sampler — the same instinct as _freeze on this site.




Soccer: Bayesian World Cup prediction





Europe versus South America, worked as a causal problem before a predictive one. Currently at stage one: the causal DAG, the implied conditional independencies, and an explicit identification statement, with latent team strength modelled as an unobserved node.
Early and incomplete — the DAG and its validation exist, the model does not yet. It is here because the ordering is the point: the identification argument is written down before anything is fitted.

title: Projects
section: Software built for someone else to use
text:
Software built for someone else to use

ATBU Academic Planning Portal





A desktop application managing 223 professor records for the Director of Academic Planning at Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University. Python and Flet over SQLite, packaged as a Windows executable for a non-technical user.
The part that mattered was the export: the National Universities Commission requires a specific Excel layout for professor-list updates, and producing it by hand for accreditation is where the errors were coming from. The app generates it directly, and imports the three-section Excel format the university already used. Editing is password-protected with bcrypt, and the database backs up in one click.




PRP Command Center





A single-file, zero-dependency operations dashboard covering 20 local government areas and 212 wards in Bauchi State, with real GRID3 geography rendered as inline SVG.
The constraint drove the design: no network requests at all, so it works on a laptop in a room with no connection, which is the room it was built for. Ward status is derived from the clock rather than fetched.




Kaduna Solar Lead Gen





A Streamlit app that pulls real business locations from OpenStreetMap and turns them into qualified solar-installation leads with a generated pitch per prospect.

title: The standard error, rewritten without the sampling-distribution detour
text:
Open almost any introductory text at the standard error and you meet the same three-step construction: imagine drawing your sample again, and again, forever; imagine the mean of each of those samples; the standard error is the standard deviation of that imagined collection.
It is correct. It is also the point at which a large fraction of readers silently stop following, because the object being described does not exist and never will. You have one sample. You will never draw another.
This is a rewrite of that section without the detour.

title: The standard error, rewritten without the sampling-distribution detour
section: Start from the question people actually have
text:
Start from the question people actually have
The question is not “what would happen across infinite repetitions.” It is:

I computed a mean of 4.2. How far off is it likely to be?

That question is answerable directly, and the answer is the standard error. So say that first, and derive it second.

title: The standard error, rewritten without the sampling-distribution detour
text:
The plain statement
The standard error is a distance. It is roughly how far your estimate sits from the truth, in the units of the thing you measured.
If you measured height in centimetres and the standard error of the mean is 1.3, then your estimate is typically off by something on the order of 1.3 cm. Not exactly 1.3 — typically around it. That is the whole idea, and everything after it is detail about how to compute the number and how much to trust it.

title: The standard error, rewritten without the sampling-distribution detour
section: Why it shrinks with more data, without algebra
text:
Why it shrinks with more data, without algebra
Individual measurements disagree with each other. When you average them, the disagreements partially cancel: some measurements were high, some low, and the average lands somewhere in between the errors rather than inheriting the worst of them.
More measurements means more cancellation. That is why the standard error gets smaller as the sample grows.
It does not shrink proportionally to the sample size, though, and this is the part worth stating explicitly because it is where practical decisions go wrong. Cancellation has diminishing returns: the second observation cancels a lot against the first, the two-hundredth cancels very little against the other hundred and ninety-nine. Concretely — to halve the standard error you need four times the data. Not twice.
That single sentence does more work in a study-design meeting than the formula does. It belongs before the formula, not after it.

title: The standard error, rewritten without the sampling-distribution detour
text:
Now the formula
\[
\text{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
where \(s\) is the standard deviation of your measurements and \(n\) is how many you have.
Read it as: start with how much individual measurements disagree, then reduce that by how much averaging cancels. The \(\sqrt{n}\) in the denominator is the diminishing-returns fact from the previous section, written down. The formula is the summary of the idea, not the source of it.

title: The standard error, rewritten without the sampling-distribution detour
section: Standard deviation vs standard error, said once, clearly
text:
Standard deviation vs standard error, said once, clearly
These are confused constantly, and the confusion is usually blamed on students when it is actually caused by introducing both in the same paragraph with similar names.

The standard deviation describes the data. If you measured heights, it says how much people’s heights differ from each other. Collecting more data does not make it smaller — it makes it more accurately known. People do not become more similar because you measured more of them.
The standard error describes your estimate. It says how far your computed average is likely to be from the true average. Collecting more data does make it smaller, because the average gets more reliable.

One sentence test: if the number would stay about the same after you doubled your sample, it is a standard deviation. If it would shrink, it is a standard error.

title: The standard error, rewritten without the sampling-distribution detour
text:
Where the sampling distribution goes
It does not disappear — it becomes the justification, which is where it belongs, rather than the introduction, where it does not.
Once a reader knows what the standard error is for and roughly how it behaves, the repeated-sampling argument is no longer a barrier to entry. It is a proof that the number means what it was already claimed to mean, and readers who want that proof can now follow it, because they know what it is proving.

title: The standard error, rewritten without the sampling-distribution detour
text:
What this rewrite gives up
Precision, in two places, deliberately:

“Typically off by about the standard error” is loose. The exact statement involves a distribution and a coverage probability. The loose version is right in the way that matters for a first pass, and the exact one is a paragraph away for anyone who wants it.
\(s/\sqrt{n}\) assumes the observations are independent. Clustered or correlated data breaks it, sometimes badly, and a rewrite aimed at beginners should flag that rather than quietly rely on it. The flag is more useful than the correction at this stage — knowing the assumption exists is what stops someone applying the formula to repeated measures on the same subjects.

title: The standard error, rewritten without the sampling-distribution detour
text:
Companion simulation
The diminishing-returns claim — four times the data to halve the error — is worth seeing rather than being told. That is a simulation post rather than a prose one, and it will be linked here when it exists.

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
A poll interviews two thousand people and reports a number for a country of ninety million. The objection writes itself: two thousand is a rounding error against ninety million, so how can it say anything?
Accuracy comes from the absolute size of the sample, not from the fraction of the population it covers. For a proportion \(p\) estimated from \(n\) people drawn at random,
\[SE = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\]
in which \(N\) does not appear. It enters once, through the finite population correction:
\[SE_{\text{fpc}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \times \sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}\]
That second square root is population size’s entire contribution, and it bites only when \(n\) is a serious fraction of \(N\): \(n\) buys precision, not \(n/N\). So say Freedman, Pisani and Purves, on chance errors in sampling.
That is the half people argue about. The half that decides elections is whether the spoon reached the whole pot, which no arithmetic on a poll that already missed can settle. So this ends in an invented country, where the answer is fixed before anyone is interviewed.
Codelibrary(plotly)

comma <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  formatC(x, format = "f", big.mark = ",", digits = digits)
}

z <- qnorm(0.975)                        # 95% two-sided

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
The translation


The standard error describes variance around \(\mathbb{E}[\hat p]\), not the distance from \(\hat p\) to \(p\). If the frame excludes part of the population then \(\mathbb{E}[\hat p] \neq p\), and that gap is unaffected by \(n\).


A cook tasting soup needs no bigger spoon for a bigger pot, so long as the pot is stirred. Stirring is the assumption, and the one that breaks. If the spoon only reaches the top, a bigger spoon reads the top more precisely and never touches the bottom. The comparison is George Gallup’s.

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
The claim
On 4 February 2023, three weeks before Nigeria voted, Nasir El-Rufai appeared on TVC’s Journalists’ Hangout and dismissed the opinion polls that showed Peter Obi ahead:

Opinion polls are distorted… When you have about a 100 million registered voters and you are sampling 2,000 registered voters or 300 registered voters, your results from day one are unreliable; they will have high margins of error.

He was right that the polls were wrong. Obi finished third. He said two other things in the same appearance, one about method:

Most of these polls, like the one by Bloomberg, ANAP and the one by Okonjo Iweala, all used telephone. What percentage of registered voters have phone numbers in INEC’s records? We have found out and it’s 31 per cent.

and one about his own numbers:

We have done a poll with a sample of nearly 40,000 across Nigeria and the result of the poll shows that we are ahead.

The poll he named is real and published, which makes it usable here. ANAP Foundation and NOIPolls interviewed two thousand registered voters by mobile phone in early February 2023, publishing the sample size and method with the numbers.

Code# ---- Quoted inputs. Every other number in this post derives from these. ----

# ANAP Foundation / NOIPolls, February 2023; see the method note below.
anap_n <- 2000
poll <- c(Obi = 21, Tinubu = 13, Atiku = 10, Kwankwaso = 3,
          Undecided = 23, Refused = 30)

elrufai_n   <- 40000    # his own poll, as he described it on air
phone_share <- 0.31     # his figure for phone coverage, not checked against INEC

# INEC, 2023 presidential election.
registered  <- 93469008
votes_cast  <- 24965218
votes_valid <- 24025940
votes <- c(Obi = 6101533, Tinubu = 8794726,
           Atiku = 6984520, Kwankwaso = 1496687)

# A mistyped input should fail the render rather than publish quietly.
stopifnot(
  sum(poll) == 100,
  sum(votes) <= votes_valid,
  votes_valid <= votes_cast,
  votes_cast <= registered
)


Fifty-three of every hundred respondents were undecided or would not say, so the headline numbers do not sum to anything like a vote share. Comparing with the result means rebasing onto the respondents who named a candidate.

Codedecided  <- sum(poll[names(votes)])
poll_obi <- poll[["Obi"]] / decided
act_obi  <- votes[["Obi"]] / votes_valid
miss     <- poll_obi - act_obi

data.frame(
  candidate = names(votes),
  polled    = sprintf("%.0f%%", poll[names(votes)]),
  rebased   = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * poll[names(votes)] / decided),
  actual    = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * votes / votes_valid)
)

  candidate polled rebased actual
1       Obi    21%  44.68% 25.40%
2    Tinubu    13%  27.66% 36.61%
3     Atiku    10%  21.28% 29.07%
4 Kwankwaso     3%   6.38%  6.23%


Rebased, the poll put Obi on 44.68% of decided respondents. He took 25.40% of valid votes. The gap is 19.29 percentage points, the largest error in the table by a distance.

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
What the objection is worth
The objection was about the ratio of two thousand to a hundred million. That ratio has exactly one place to enter the arithmetic, so it can be priced.

Codefpc     <- sqrt((registered - anap_n) / (registered - 1))
se_anap <- sqrt(poll_obi * (1 - poll_obi) / anap_n)

c(correction       = sprintf("%.7f", fpc),
  se_ignoring_pop  = sprintf("%.4f pp", 100 * se_anap),
  se_including_pop = sprintf("%.4f pp", 100 * se_anap * fpc),
  shrinkage        = sprintf("%.4f%%", 100 * (1 - fpc)))

      correction  se_ignoring_pop se_including_pop        shrinkage 
     "0.9999893"      "1.1117 pp"      "1.1117 pp"        "0.0011%" 


The correction is 0.9999893. Knowing the population is 93,469,008 rather than unlimited improves the poll’s standard error by 0.0011% of itself. That is the whole effect of population size here, and the entire content of the objection.

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
The size of the miss
The margin of error says how far the estimate would wander if you ran the poll again. The miss is how far it was from the answer. One in units of the other says whether sample size is a plausible explanation.

Code# The sample size at which the margin of error would have been as wide as the
# miss, i.e. the only n for which the objection lands.
n_cross <- ceiling(z^2 * poll_obi * (1 - poll_obi) / miss^2)

c(miss          = sprintf("%.2f pp", 100 * miss),
  miss_in_se    = sprintf("%.1f", miss / se_anap),
  n_for_margin  = comma(n_cross),
  times_smaller = sprintf("%.0f", anap_n / n_cross))

         miss    miss_in_se  n_for_margin times_smaller 
   "19.29 pp"        "17.3"          "26"          "77" 


The miss was 17.3 standard errors. Sampling noise does not produce that: three is already a one-in-a-few-hundred event, and this is nearly six times further out.
Solve the margin of error backwards for the sample size that would cover it and you get 26 people, 77 times smaller than the poll run. For “your sample was too small” to explain it, the poll would have had to be a group chat. The complaint points the opposite way to the error.
Which is the point about his second sentence. The 31 per cent is about the frame, not the sample, and a frame missing two thirds of the register is the one objection on the table that no increase in \(n\) can answer. He had the correct argument, and it went unquoted.

title: How big should the spoon be?
section: A country where we know the answer
text:
A country where we know the answer
Everything above works backwards, pricing the objection against a miss after the fact. It cannot check whether the method finds the right answer, because in the real case the result was the only truth available and it arrived three weeks late.
So here is a country where the truth is fixed first. NaijaSim has ninety million registered voters, six zones of two states each, and four parties named after colours so that nothing reads as a claim about a person. The zone names are real and nothing else is. One thing is borrowed, the one the argument turns on: phone coverage is his 31%.

Codeset.seed(20260817)

sim_party <- c("Green", "Blue", "Red", "Yellow")
sim_zone  <- c("North West", "North East", "North Central",
               "South West", "South East", "South South")
sim_reg_z <- c(21, 12, 15, 18, 9, 15) * 1e6      # registered voters, by zone
names(sim_reg_z) <- sim_zone

# The national result, set by fiat. Blue wins.
sim_target <- c(Green = 0.30, Blue = 0.38, Red = 0.24, Yellow = 0.08)

# Zone shares are chosen, EXCEPT North Central, solved so the register-weighted
# truth lands exactly on sim_target.
sim_zs <- rbind(
  c(0.08, 0.50, 0.36, 0.06),
  c(0.10, 0.52, 0.32, 0.06),
  c(NA,   NA,   NA,   NA  ),
  c(0.34, 0.34, 0.22, 0.10),
  c(0.72, 0.12, 0.08, 0.08),
  c(0.48, 0.26, 0.16, 0.10)
)
dimnames(sim_zs) <- list(sim_zone, sim_party)
i_nc <- match("North Central", sim_zone)
sim_zs[i_nc, ] <- (sum(sim_reg_z) * sim_target -
                   colSums(sim_zs[-i_nc, ] * sim_reg_z[-i_nc])) / sim_reg_z[i_nc]

# Phone reach is chosen, EXCEPT South South, solved so national coverage is
# exactly the 31 per cent he quoted. The poorest zones reach fewest.
sim_reach_z <- c(`North West` = 0.160, `North East` = 0.120,
                 `North Central` = 0.300, `South West` = 0.500,
                 `South East` = 0.440, `South South` = NA)[sim_zone]
i_ss <- match("South South", sim_zone)
sim_reach_z[i_ss] <- (phone_share * sum(sim_reg_z) -
                      sum((sim_reg_z * sim_reach_z)[-i_ss])) / sim_reg_z[i_ss]

# Each zone splits 60/40 into two states leaning opposite ways, so no stratum is
# internally uniform. B moves 1.5x as far as A, preserving the zone average; the
# 0.5 cap keeps every state inside (0, 1).
sim_st <- NULL; sim_reg_s <- numeric(0); sim_szone <- character(0)
for (zn in sim_zone) {
  g <- sim_zs[zn, "Green"]; b <- sim_zs[zn, "Blue"]
  d <- 0.5 * min(g / 1.5, b)
  s_a <- sim_zs[zn, ]; s_a["Green"] <- g + d;       s_a["Blue"] <- b - d
  s_b <- sim_zs[zn, ]; s_b["Green"] <- g - 1.5 * d; s_b["Blue"] <- b + 1.5 * d
  sim_st    <- rbind(sim_st, s_a, s_b)
  sim_reg_s <- c(sim_reg_s, 0.60 * sim_reg_z[[zn]], 0.40 * sim_reg_z[[zn]])
  sim_szone <- c(sim_szone, zn, zn)
}
sim_frame_s <- sim_reg_s * unname(sim_reach_z[sim_szone])

# A mistyped country should fail the render rather than publish quietly.
stopifnot(
  sum(sim_reg_z) == 90e6,
  all(abs(rowSums(sim_st) - 1) < 1e-12),
  all(sim_st > 0), all(sim_st < 1),
  isTRUE(all.equal(colSums(sim_st * sim_reg_s) / sum(sim_reg_s), sim_target)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(sum(sim_frame_s) / sum(sim_reg_s), phone_share))
)

sim_w_true  <- sim_reg_s   / sum(sim_reg_s)     # a fair poll's weights
sim_w_frame <- sim_frame_s / sum(sim_frame_s)   # what a phone poll actually gets
sim_truth   <- colSums(sim_st * sim_w_true)
sim_ptruth  <- colSums(sim_st * sim_w_frame)
sim_frame_N <- sum(sim_frame_s)

data.frame(
  party            = sim_party,
  whole_register   = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * sim_truth),
  phone_frame_only = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * sim_ptruth)
)

   party whole_register phone_frame_only
1  Green         30.00%           37.02%
2   Blue         38.00%           33.47%
3    Red         24.00%           20.81%
4 Yellow          8.00%            8.71%


Blue wins NaijaSim by 8 points, the fact a poll is being asked to find.
The second column is the same country seen through a telephone. Reach is not uniform across zones and the zones do not vote alike, so the 27,900,000 voters who can be called are not a small copy of the 90,000,000 who cannot: among them Green leads by 3.54 points. Phone owners within a state vote like their neighbours here, so all of that gap is geography.
Now run the poll: stratified by state, four thousand repetitions at each setting, the register sampled at six sizes down to the 26 the inversion produced and the phone frame at the two that were quoted.

Code# Seeded here, not left to the chunk above, so these numbers do not depend on
# how many draws the country construction happened to consume.
set.seed(20260817)

# Largest remainder: proportional shares rounded the obvious way do not sum to n.
sim_alloc <- function(n, w) {
  raw <- n * w; a <- floor(raw); k <- n - sum(a)
  if (k > 0) { j <- order(raw - a, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(k)]; a[j] <- a[j] + 1 }
  stopifnot(sum(a) == n)
  a
}

SIM_REPS <- 4000

# One rmultinom call per state, vectorised over all 4,000 repetitions.
sim_run <- function(n, w) {
  a <- sim_alloc(n, w)
  est <- matrix(0, SIM_REPS, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, sim_party))
  for (i in seq_along(a)) {
    if (a[i] == 0) next
    est <- est + w[i] * t(rmultinom(SIM_REPS, a[i], sim_st[i, ])) / a[i]
  }
  est
}

# "Right" means Blue tops the poll, not merely Blue ahead of Green.
sim_summ <- function(est) {
  g <- 100 * est[, "Green"]
  c(green = mean(g), sd = sd(g),
    right = 100 * mean(sim_party[max.col(est, ties.method = "first")] == "Blue"))
}

# 100.0% is also what 99.95% prints as, so the prose quotes counts, derived here.
sim_wrong <- function(pct_right) round(SIM_REPS * (100 - pct_right) / 100)

sim_ns_fair  <- c(n_cross, 100, 250, 500, 1000, anap_n)
sim_ns_phone <- c(anap_n, elrufai_n)
sim_fair  <- lapply(sim_ns_fair,  sim_run, w = sim_w_true)
sim_phone <- lapply(sim_ns_phone, sim_run, w = sim_w_frame)
sim_ft    <- t(sapply(sim_fair,  sim_summ))
sim_pt    <- t(sapply(sim_phone, sim_summ))

# Indexed by value, not position, so the prose survives a reordered ladder.
i_win <- match(500, sim_ns_fair)     # the rung the argument turns on
i_2k  <- match(anap_n, sim_ns_fair)
j_2k  <- match(anap_n, sim_ns_phone)
j_40k <- match(elrufai_n, sim_ns_phone)

data.frame(
  drawn_from   = rep(c("whole register", "phone frame"),
                     c(length(sim_ns_fair), length(sim_ns_phone))),
  interviews   = comma(c(sim_ns_fair, sim_ns_phone)),
  green_says   = sprintf("%.2f%%", c(sim_ft[, "green"], sim_pt[, "green"])),
  wobble       = sprintf("%.2f pp", c(sim_ft[, "sd"], sim_pt[, "sd"])),
  winner_right = sprintf("%.1f%%", c(sim_ft[, "right"], sim_pt[, "right"]))
)

      drawn_from interviews green_says  wobble winner_right
1 whole register         26     30.17% 7.82 pp        64.1%
2 whole register        100     30.06% 4.04 pp        84.8%
3 whole register        250     29.98% 2.50 pp        96.5%
4 whole register        500     29.98% 1.78 pp        99.2%
5 whole register      1,000     30.00% 1.27 pp       100.0%
6 whole register      2,000     30.01% 0.87 pp       100.0%
7    phone frame      2,000     37.02% 0.96 pp         1.5%
8    phone frame     40,000     37.01% 0.21 pp         0.0%


Read the last column.
500 interviews drawn from the whole register name the winner in 3,967 of 4,000 runs. 40,000 drawn from the phone frame name it in 0. The winning poll is 80 times smaller, and wins on where its sample came from, not how big it was.
The ladder fills in the shape. Even 26 interviews, the group chat from two sections ago, get the winner right 64.1% of the time. The phone frame never climbs: 2,000 interviews pick the wrong winner 3,941 times out of 4,000, and twenty times the interviewing leaves that at 4,000. Meanwhile the wobble column does what the formula at the top promises: the scatter falls with the square root of the sample size. Every bit of precision the phone frame buys is spent stating the wrong answer more firmly.







Figure 1: Where the poll lands over four thousand repetitions. Drawn from the whole register it sits on the truth, loosely at five hundred interviews and tightly at two thousand. Drawn from the phone frame it sits seven points away, and forty thousand interviews sit in the same wrong place with the least scatter on the chart. Each curve is scaled to its own peak.



The shape of the failure is the point. “Unreliable” is normally taken to mean wide. The phone poll at 2,000 scatters 0.96 of a point against the fair poll’s 0.87 at the same sample size, and the 40,000 curve is the narrowest on the chart. Width is not what is wrong with them: they are in the wrong place, and the arithmetic that governs width says nothing about position.


Dem ask 500 people and dem sabi? The other one ask 40,000 o.

Yes, and the five hundred got it right, the forty thousand wrong, every time. Forty thousand is a bigger spoon, not a longer one: if it never reaches past the top of the pot, the extra size only buys the wrong answer to more decimal places.

One aside, because it cuts against the original complaint from a second direction. The observed scatter at 2,000 interviews is 0.87 of a point, against the simple-random formula’s 1.02. Stratifying by state removes the between-state variation, so the poll’s method is slightly more precise than the textbook number it was attacked with.






NoteWhere the numbers come from



Quoted, not derived. The El-Rufai quotations are as reported by The Guardian Nigeria from Journalists’ Hangout on TVC News, 4 February 2023. The sample size, phone-based stratified random method and the six percentages come from ANAP Foundation’s press release; the register, votes and candidate totals are INEC’s, via the published breakdown. Outlets differ on the second figure in that first quotation, The Guardian having “300” where The Cable reports “three thousand”; the arithmetic uses ANAP’s published 2,000, so nothing turns on it. His own 40,000-sample poll has no published methodology I could find, and appears here as a sample size and nothing else.
Attribution, split deliberately. That accuracy depends on absolute sample size rather than on the sampling fraction is standard, and Freedman, Pisani and Purves develop it in the chapter on chance errors in sampling in Statistics. The soup-and-spoon comparison is attributed to George Gallup, not to them, because I could not verify that the book uses the soup wording.
NaijaSim is invented, and deliberately not a model of Nigeria. Its zone names are real; its register, zone splits, parties and result are made up. Verifiable zone-level figures for 2023 from a single authoritative source do not exist, and inventing them while calling them the past would be worse than inventing a country and saying so. Only its coverage figure of 31% and three sample sizes come from the real case: 2,000, 40,000, and the 26 the inversion produced. It is seeded, so the figures reproduce exactly.

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
What this does not show
Four things are doing real work, and several of them cut against the post.
The poll was wrong. Nothing above defends its finding. It defends its sample size, which is a different object. A poll can be built correctly at the scale it claims and still land 17.3 standard errors from the answer, and this one did.
The 53% who did not answer are carrying the argument. Rebasing onto decided respondents assumes the silent half would have split like the vocal half. That is the largest assumption on this page, and it is plainly false. A different assumption moves 44.68% a long way.
The 31 per cent is his figure, not a verified one. It is quoted as his claim about INEC’s records and used only to size an illustration. If true coverage is higher the frame problem is smaller than the simulation implies, though it would have to be very much higher to stop being the better objection.
NaijaSim’s coverage gap was set to a size that flips the winner. That is the honest limit of it. Different reach figures produce a phone frame that gets the answer right, and I chose ones that do not. It shows a coverage gap of the size he described is sufficient to produce a confident wrong answer that more interviewing cannot fix, not that this happened to the ANAP poll. It also assumes phone owners within a state vote like their neighbours, when real bias runs by age and income too; that everyone answers, and answers honestly, where the real poll had 53% who did neither; and that nobody changes their mind.
What survives all four is the shape. Population size entered this poll’s arithmetic once, through a term worth 0.0011%, and the error was 17.3 standard errors. Whatever went wrong here, the number of people interviewed was not it.

title: Separation makes logistic regression fail loudly in the warnings and quietly in the estimates
text:
When a predictor separates a binary outcome perfectly, the logistic regression maximum likelihood estimate does not exist. The likelihood keeps increasing as the coefficient grows, so the optimiser stops at whatever its convergence rule happens to hit. The reported number is an artefact of the stopping rule.
R does warn, but it warns about the wrong thing: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred describes a symptom on the probability scale. The coefficient and its standard error — the two numbers that end up in a table — come back with no annotation at all.
This post simulates the approach to separation so you can watch both quantities go.

title: Separation makes logistic regression fail loudly in the warnings and quietly in the estimates
text:
Setup

Codelibrary(ggplot2)
library(ggiraph)
library(plotly)

set.seed(20260812)

title: Separation makes logistic regression fail loudly in the warnings and quietly in the estimates
text:
Simulating the approach to separation
One predictor, one binary outcome. The parameter beta controls how sharply the outcome tracks the predictor: at beta = 0.5 the classes overlap heavily, and as beta grows the boundary sharpens until — in any finite sample — the two classes stop overlapping at all. That last state is separation, and it arrives by degrees rather than all at once.

Codesimulate_once <- function(beta, n = 200) {
  x <- rnorm(n)
  y <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = plogis(beta * x))
  data.frame(x = x, y = y)
}

# `glm` warns about fitted probabilities near separation; that warning is the
# subject of this post rather than a problem with the call, so it is captured
# rather than printed 40 times.
fit_once <- function(beta) {
  d <- simulate_once(beta)
  warned <- FALSE
  m <- withCallingHandlers(
    glm(y ~ x, data = d, family = binomial),
    warning = function(w) {
      warned <<- TRUE
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }
  )
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  overlap <- min(max(d$x[d$y == 0]), max(d$x[d$y == 1])) -
    max(min(d$x[d$y == 0]), min(d$x[d$y == 1]))

  data.frame(
    beta_true = beta,
    estimate  = co["x", "Estimate"],
    se        = co["x", "Std. Error"],
    warned    = warned,
    overlap   = overlap
  )
}

betas <- seq(0.5, 18, length.out = 45)
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(betas, fit_once))

title: Separation makes logistic regression fail loudly in the warnings and quietly in the estimates
text:
The estimate
Hover any point for the fitted values. Points where R issued a warning are marked.

Coderes$tooltip <- sprintf(
  "true beta: %.1f\nestimate: %.2f\nstd. error: %.2f\nR warned: %s",
  res$beta_true, res$estimate, res$se, ifelse(res$warned, "yes", "no")
)

p <- ggplot(res, aes(beta_true, estimate)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = tooltip, data_id = beta_true, colour = warned),
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#0f766e", "TRUE" = "#b45309"),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "no warning", "TRUE" = "R warned"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(x = "true coefficient", y = "estimated coefficient") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 7,
  height_svg = 4.2,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = "fill:#c026d3;stroke:none;r:5pt;"),
    opts_tooltip(css = "background:#111;color:#eee;padding:6px;border-radius:4px;font-family:monospace;font-size:12px;")
  )
)






Figure 1: Estimated coefficient against its true value. The diagonal is where an unbiased estimator would sit.



The estimate tracks the truth while the classes still overlap and then comes apart. Past the point where a sample happens to be separable, the estimate is reporting the optimiser’s patience, not the data.

title: Separation makes logistic regression fail loudly in the warnings and quietly in the estimates
text:
The standard error
The standard error is the more dangerous of the two, because it moves in the direction that looks like caution:

Codeq <- ggplot(res, aes(beta_true, se, colour = warned)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#0f766e", "TRUE" = "#b45309"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(x = "true coefficient", y = "standard error (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

ggplotly(q, tooltip = c("x", "y"))






Figure 2: Standard error of the coefficient. Note the log scale — this is not a gentle increase.



A huge standard error produces a wide confidence interval and a p-value nowhere near significance. Read casually, that says “not enough evidence” — the exact opposite of what is happening, which is that the predictor is so strongly associated with the outcome that the model cannot express it.

title: Separation makes logistic regression fail loudly in the warnings and quietly in the estimates
text:
What this does not show
This is one predictor, one sample per setting, and no repetition — so the wiggle between adjacent points is sampling noise, not structure. The qualitative behaviour (divergence, exploding standard error) is a property of the likelihood and does not depend on the seed; the specific value of beta where it starts does, because whether a given sample is separable is itself random.
The fix is not shown here. Penalised likelihood (Firth) and a weakly informative prior both give finite estimates under separation, and comparing them is its own post.

title: A Normal(0, 10) prior on a logistic coefficient is not weak — it is a confident bet on certainty
text:
“Weakly informative” is a claim about what a prior implies, and the log-odds scale is not where that claim can be checked. A coefficient prior of Normal(0, 10) looks generous — ten units of log-odds either way, why would that constrain anything.
Push it through the inverse logit and it becomes a different statement: a one standard-deviation change in this predictor almost certainly moves the outcome from near-impossible to near-certain. That is not vague. It is a strong and usually wrong belief, held accidentally.
The check takes about fifteen lines.

title: A Normal(0, 10) prior on a logistic coefficient is not weak — it is a confident bet on certainty
text:
Setup


Code
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

rng = np.random.default_rng(20260812)
N_DRAWS = 60_000

def inv_logit(z):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))

def rgba(hex_colour, alpha):
    h = hex_colour.lstrip("#")
    r, g, b = (int(h[i:i + 2], 16) for i in (0, 2, 4))
    return f"rgba({r},{g},{b},{alpha})"

# Bin here rather than handing plotly the raw draws. go.Histogram ships every
# value to the browser and bins client-side, which for 60,000 draws x 3 priors
# x 2 figures is ~7 MB of JSON embedded in the page. Binning first sends 80
# numbers per curve and draws exactly the same picture.
def density_curve(values, lo=0.0, hi=1.0, n_bins=80):
    counts, edges = np.histogram(values, bins=np.linspace(lo, hi, n_bins + 1), density=True)
    centres = 0.5 * (edges[:-1] + edges[1:])
    return centres, counts

title: A Normal(0, 10) prior on a logistic coefficient is not weak — it is a confident bet on certainty
section: The implied prior on a probability
text:
The implied prior on a probability
Take a predictor standardised to unit variance and a baseline log-odds of zero, so the model is p = inv_logit(beta * x). Evaluating at x = 1 — a one-standard-deviation change, an ordinary amount of movement — the prior on beta induces a prior on p.


Code
prior_sds = {"Normal(0, 1)": 1.0, "Normal(0, 2.5)": 2.5, "Normal(0, 10)": 10.0}

implied = {
    name: inv_logit(rng.normal(0.0, sd, N_DRAWS))
    for name, sd in prior_sds.items()
}




Code
colors = {"Normal(0, 1)": "#0f766e", "Normal(0, 2.5)": "#b45309", "Normal(0, 10)": "#6d28d9"}

fig = go.Figure()
for name, draws in implied.items():
    x, y = density_curve(draws)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x,
        y=y,
        name=name,
        mode="lines",
        line=dict(color=colors[name], width=2),
        fill="tozeroy",
        fillcolor=rgba(colors[name], 0.22),
        hovertemplate="p ≈ %{x:.2f}<br>density %{y:.2f}<extra>" + name + "</extra>",
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="implied probability of the outcome",
    yaxis_title="prior density",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.12, x=0),
    margin=dict(l=50, r=20, t=40, b=50),
    height=420,
    template="simple_white",
)
fig.show()




                                                


Figure 1: Implied prior on the outcome probability at a one-SD change in the predictor. A genuinely uninformative prior would be roughly flat across this range.




Normal(0, 10) is the U-shaped one. It does not spread belief across probabilities — it concentrates it at the two extremes and leaves the middle, where nearly every real effect lives, almost empty.

title: A Normal(0, 10) prior on a logistic coefficient is not weak — it is a confident bet on certainty
section: How much mass sits at the extremes
text:
How much mass sits at the extremes


Code
rows = []
for name, draws in implied.items():
    rows.append({
        "prior on β": name,
        "P(p < 0.01)": np.mean(draws < 0.01),
        "P(p > 0.99)": np.mean(draws > 0.99),
        "P(0.2 < p < 0.8)": np.mean((draws > 0.2) & (draws < 0.8)),
    })

pd.DataFrame(rows).style.format({
    "P(p < 0.01)": "{:.1%}",

Under Normal(0, 10), roughly two thirds of the prior mass says the outcome is practically determined, and only a small slice allows a moderate probability. Under Normal(0, 1) most of the mass is in the moderate range, which is what “weakly informative” is supposed to mean.

title: A Normal(0, 10) prior on a logistic coefficient is not weak — it is a confident bet on certainty
section: The same problem on the risk-difference scale
text:
The same problem on the risk-difference scale
Coefficients are rarely what a reader wants; the change in probability is. So put an ordinary prior on the intercept as well and look at what the model believes about the effect size before seeing any data.


Code
alpha = rng.normal(0.0, 1.5, N_DRAWS)

fig2 = go.Figure()
for name, sd in prior_sds.items():
    beta = rng.normal(0.0, sd, N_DRAWS)
    risk_diff = np.abs(inv_logit(alpha + beta) - inv_logit(alpha))
    x, y = density_curve(risk_diff)
    fig2.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x,
        y=y,
        name=name,
        mode="lines",
        line=dict(color=colors[name], width=2),
        fill="tozeroy",
        fillcolor=rgba(colors[name], 0.22),
        hovertemplate="|Δp| ≈ %{x:.2f}<br>density %{y:.2f}<extra>" + name + "</extra>",
    ))
    # Dashed line at the median, since that is the claim the text makes.
    fig2.add_vline(
        x=float(np.median(risk_diff)),
        line=dict(color=colors[name], width=1.5, dash="dash"),
    )

fig2.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="absolute change in probability, |Δp|  (dashed line = median)",
    yaxis_title="prior density",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.12, x=0),
    margin=dict(l=50, r=20, t=40, b=50),
    height=400,
    template="simple_white",
)
fig2.show()




                                                


Figure 2: Implied prior on the absolute change in probability from x = 0 to x = 1. Interactive — drag to zoom, double-click to reset.




The wide prior’s median belief is that the predictor swings the outcome probability by most of its available range. Stated in words, nobody would assert that. Stated as Normal(0, 10), people assert it routinely.

title: A Normal(0, 10) prior on a logistic coefficient is not weak — it is a confident bet on certainty
text:
What this does not show

The predictor is standardised. On an unstandardised predictor the same prior means something else entirely, which is a separate reason wide priors on raw covariates go wrong.
With enough data the likelihood dominates and the prior stops mattering much. The argument here is about the small-and-sparse case — rare outcomes, interactions, hierarchical terms with few groups — where it does not.
Nothing here says Normal(0, 1) is correct. It says the check should be run on the scale you actually have beliefs about, and then the prior chosen.

title: Simulations
text:
A prior is a claim about what data is plausible. That claim can be simulated, looked at, and rejected — before any real observation is involved. These posts do that, and also take the wider case: run a method against assumptions it does not hold and see precisely where it bends.
















A Normal(0, 10) prior on a logistic coefficient is not weak — it is a confident bet on certainty



prior-sims



Priors are chosen on the log-odds scale and interpreted as vague. Pushed through the inverse logit, a wide Normal prior puts most of its mass on probabilities of essentially 0 or essentially 1.
